findings.reason: The protected SQL solution forms valid country triplets by CROSS JOINing SchoolA, SchoolB, and SchoolC. It filters out rows where student_id or student_name are equal between any pair of schools (A-B, A-C, B-C). The query runs in O(a * b * c) time and O(a * b * c) space; no candidate is required.
6 inequality predicates (3 for student_id and 3 for student_name) guarantee that every returned triplet contains 3 pairwise distinct IDs and 3 pairwise distinct names.

Evaluating a x b x c candidate triplets with 6 constant-time inequality checks takes O(a * b * c) time and O(a * b * c) space for the result set. Complexity evidence is bounded-domain certified and hash-bound.
Accepts SchoolA, SchoolB, and SchoolC tables and returns columns member_A, member_B, and member_C.

The approach accurately details Cartesian product generation, 6-way pairwise inequality enforcement, member name aliased projections, and O(a * b * c) time/space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover inner join equivalence, NOT IN subquery limitations, ID-only vs name-only comparison pitfalls, A-C collision detection, empty school table handling, and member sharing across different valid triplets.

App SQL and native SQL solutions both execute the identical CROSS JOIN 6-way inequality query with SHA-256 digest 5ceb79ad57013e06c0d0fab094cf5504ce3d397ef9c0d9046292c7b473f36549. Verified submission remains untouched.

Statement structure and factual evidence confirmed SchoolA, SchoolB, and SchoolC interface, three examples, three constraints, and 2 local tables. Bound to content SHA-256 f664f3fcf4447d4c2472c9e017471858bb4799b05c7420a91fd1e917f71df270.
